passage:
Contract law has long recognized the principle of unconscionability, which permits courts to refuse enforcement of a contract or particular clause when the bargain is so one-sided that it shocks the conscience. This principle emerged in the common law tradition as a safeguard against exploitation in transactions where one party holds vastly superior bargaining power. The doctrine of unconscionability operates on the premise that contracts, while generally enforceable according to their terms, must reflect a minimum degree of fairness between the parties.

Unconscionability is typically divided into two categories: procedural and substantive. Procedural unconscionability focuses on the manner in which a contract was formed—whether one party was deceived, had limited opportunity to read or understand the agreement, or lacked meaningful choice. Substantive unconscionability, by contrast, examines the actual terms of the contract itself, asking whether the obligations imposed on one party are unreasonably favorable to the other. Courts have found substantive unconscionability in cases involving exorbitant prices, unlimited liability clauses, or terms that deprive a party of essential remedies.

Applying unconscionability doctrine has proven challenging, however. Courts must balance the principle against the fundamental freedom of contract—the notion that parties should be free to agree to whatever terms they choose, no matter how disadvantageous to one side. A court that too readily invokes unconscionability risks substituting its judgment for that of the parties themselves. Yet a court that seldom applies the doctrine may permit unscrupulous merchants to exploit desperate consumers. This tension remains unresolved in jurisprudence, and different jurisdictions have adopted varying approaches to determining when unconscionability is truly present.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Procedural unconscionability is more important than substantive unconscionability in contract law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The doctrine of unconscionability exists to protect parties from unfair contracts, but courts face difficulty in applying it consistently with the principle of freedom of contract.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Common law has eliminated the problem of exploitation in contracts by establishing unconscionability doctrine.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Courts should always refuse to enforce contracts that contain one-sided terms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most jurisdictions have successfully resolved the tension between unconscionability and freedom of contract.

explanations.correct: The passage opens with the purpose of unconscionability (protect against exploitation), explains its two forms, and concludes by identifying the ongoing tension between applying it and respecting freedom of contract.
explanations.A: The passage does not rank procedural over substantive unconscionability; both are described neutrally.
explanations.C: Too strong—the passage says the principle 'emerged as a safeguard,' not that it has eliminated exploitation.
explanations.D: The passage does not say courts should always refuse; it discusses the difficulty of consistent application.
explanations.E: The passage explicitly states this tension 'remains unresolved,' not that most jurisdictions have resolved it.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, procedural unconscionability differs from substantive unconscionability in that procedural unconscionability concerns itself with which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The actual terms of the contract and whether they are unreasonably favorable to one party.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The manner in which a contract was formed and the degree of choice available to the parties.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The historical origins of the contract in common law tradition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The extent to which the contract eliminates remedies available to either party.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether the price stated in the contract is reasonable and fair to both parties.

explanations.correct: The passage states procedural unconscionability 'focuses on the manner in which a contract was formed—whether one party was deceived, had limited opportunity to read or understand the agreement, or lacked meaningful choice.'
explanations.A: This describes substantive unconscionability, not procedural.
explanations.C: The passage does not discuss procedural unconscionability in terms of historical origins.
explanations.D: Unlimited liability clauses and deprivation of remedies are examples of substantive unconscionability.
explanations.E: Price reasonableness is mentioned as an example of substantive, not procedural, unconscionability.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the principle of unconscionability can best be described as:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enthusiastically endorsing it as the best solution to contract disputes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Skeptical of its value in protecting vulnerable parties.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Recognizing its importance while acknowledging the difficulty of consistent application.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hostile to its limitations on freedom of contract.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Indifferent to whether courts apply unconscionability or freedom of contract principles.

explanations.correct: The author describes unconscionability as a necessary safeguard (positive view) but devotes the final paragraph to the tension it creates with freedom of contract (acknowledges difficulty).
explanations.A: The passage is measured and identifies problems with application, not enthusiastic.
explanations.B: The author presents unconscionability as protecting vulnerable parties, not skeptical of this.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The author does not portray unconscionability as hostile; rather, the tension is presented as a genuine dilemma.
explanations.E: The author clearly cares about the tension, so 'indifferent' is incorrect.

questions.questionStem: Based on the passage, it can be inferred that:

choices.label: A
choices.text: All contracts that contain terms favoring one party are unconscionable and unenforceable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Without the doctrine of unconscionability, some parties would be able to exploit others through grossly unfair contract terms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Procedural unconscionability never occurs in contracts between merchants.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The common law has entirely eliminated the tension between unconscionability and freedom of contract.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Courts are prohibited from considering freedom of contract when applying unconscionability doctrine.

explanations.correct: The passage states that unconscionability 'emerged in the common law tradition as a safeguard against exploitation' and discusses the risk of not applying it adequately ('permit unscrupulous merchants to exploit desperate consumers').
explanations.A: Too absolute—the passage discusses context-dependent application, not all such contracts.
explanations.C: The passage does not limit procedural unconscionability to any particular party type.
explanations.D: The passage explicitly states this tension 'remains unresolved.'
explanations.E: The passage indicates courts must balance unconscionability against freedom of contract, not ignore one.

questions.questionStem: The passage is organized primarily by:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Presenting a historical overview of contract law followed by modern case examples.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Introducing a legal doctrine, explaining its two categories, and then discussing challenges in its application.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Criticizing procedural unconscionability and then defending substantive unconscionability.

choices.label: D

choices.label: E
choices.text: Arguing that freedom of contract is more important than unconscionability doctrine.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces unconscionability, paragraph 2 explains its two categories, and paragraph 3 discusses the difficulty of applying it consistently.
explanations.A: The passage discusses legal principles but does not provide historical overview or modern case examples.
explanations.C: The passage does not criticize procedural over substantive unconscionability.
explanations.D: Common law and civil law systems are not compared in this passage.
explanations.E: The passage presents this as a tension, not an argument that freedom of contract is superior.

questions.questionStem: The author's mention of 'exorbitant prices, unlimited liability clauses, or terms that deprive a party of essential remedies' serves primarily to:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Argue that procedural unconscionability should never be applied.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Illustrate specific examples of what substantive unconscionability addresses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Demonstrate that all contracts contain unconscionable terms.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Show that common law was effective at preventing unfair contracts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prove that freedom of contract should be abandoned entirely.

explanations.correct: These examples appear immediately after the definition of substantive unconscionability and serve to clarify what that category includes.
explanations.A: The examples relate to substantive, not procedural, unconscionability.
explanations.C: The examples illustrate types of terms that courts have found unconscionable, not that all contracts contain them.
explanations.D: The examples describe a legal doctrine, not its historical effectiveness.
explanations.E: The examples address specific contractual terms, not the merits of freedom of contract generally.

questions.questionStem: The passage states that the doctrine of unconscionability emerged in order to:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Provide absolute protection from all unfair contract terms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eliminate the concept of freedom of contract.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serve as a safeguard against exploitation in transactions involving unequal bargaining power.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restrict contracts only to those between merchants of equal standing.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Replace common law with a new statutory framework.

explanations.correct: The passage explicitly states the doctrine 'emerged in the common law tradition as a safeguard against exploitation in transactions where one party holds vastly superior bargaining power.'
explanations.A: Absolute protection is not claimed; the doctrine serves as a safeguard.
explanations.B: The passage discusses tension with freedom of contract, not its elimination.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The passage does not restrict the doctrine to merchant-to-merchant transactions.
explanations.E: The doctrine is presented as an evolution within common law, not a replacement.

passage:
Administrative law governs the powers and procedures of government agencies and sets boundaries on how those agencies may exercise their authority. A central principle in administrative law is the requirement that agencies act within the scope of their statutory mandate—that is, the authority granted to them by the legislature. This principle is known as the doctrine of ultra vires, which prohibits agencies from exceeding the powers conferred upon them by statute.

When an agency action is challenged as ultra vires, a court must determine whether the agency had legal authority to take that action. This determination requires courts to interpret the relevant statute and assess whether the challenged action falls within the scope of the agency's authority. Courts have developed a framework for such review, examining factors including the plain language of the statute, the legislative history and intent, and the practical consequences of the agency's interpretation. If a court concludes that an agency exceeded its statutory authority, the court may invalidate the agency's action and order it to conform to the law.

However, courts generally recognize that agencies possess expertise in their respective fields, and therefore courts often defer to reasonable agency interpretations of ambiguous statutory language. This deference, known as Chevron deference in the United States, allows agencies considerable latitude in interpreting and implementing the statutes they administer. The balance between enforcing the limits of agency authority and respecting agency expertise creates a tension that courts must navigate. When statutes are clear and unambiguous, courts apply the law strictly; but when statutes contain ambiguities, courts typically uphold agency interpretations that are reasonable and consistent with the statute's purpose.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Administrative law primarily protects agency authority from judicial interference.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The doctrine of ultra vires is the only principle that governs how courts review agency actions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Administrative law requires agencies to act within their statutory authority, and courts must balance enforcing this limit with deference to agency expertise.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Courts should always defer to agency interpretations of statutes regardless of clarity.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Agencies possess such extensive expertise that courts lack the capacity to review their actions meaningfully.

explanations.correct: The passage defines the ultra vires doctrine (agency authority constraint), explains judicial review procedures, and concludes by identifying the tension between enforcement and deference.
explanations.A: The passage describes limits on agency authority, not protection of it from courts.
explanations.B: Ultra vires is presented as a central principle, but the passage discusses additional judicial review factors.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The passage states that deference applies when statutes are ambiguous, not always.
explanations.E: The passage acknowledges agency expertise but indicates courts retain meaningful review authority.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, courts reviewing an ultra vires challenge examine all of the following EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: The plain language of the statute.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The legislative history and intent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The personal political beliefs of the agency officials who authorized the action.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The practical consequences of the agency's interpretation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether the challenged action falls within the scope of the agency's authority.

explanations.correct: The passage lists factors courts examine: plain language, legislative history, and practical consequences. Personal political beliefs are not mentioned as a review factor.
explanations.A: The passage states courts examine 'the plain language of the statute.'
explanations.B: The passage mentions 'the legislative history and intent.'
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The passage includes 'the practical consequences of the agency's interpretation.'
explanations.E: This is the core inquiry when determining ultra vires.

questions.questionStem: Based on the passage, it can be inferred that:

choices.label: A
choices.text: All agency interpretations of statutes are presumptively valid.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Courts may invalidate agency actions even when the relevant statute is ambiguous if the agency interpretation is unreasonable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Agencies never have legitimate reasons to interpret statutes in ways courts would not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The doctrine of ultra vires has been eliminated in modern administrative law.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Legislative history is more important than the plain language of a statute.

explanations.correct: The passage states that courts defer to agency interpretations that are 'reasonable and consistent with the statute's purpose'—implying unreasonable interpretations may be overturned even when statutes are ambiguous.
explanations.A: The passage indicates courts must still assess whether agency interpretations are reasonable.
explanations.C: The passage acknowledges that agencies possess expertise in their fields, suggesting legitimate interpretive authority.
explanations.D: The doctrine is presented as an ongoing principle in contemporary administrative law.
explanations.E: The passage lists these as separate factors courts examine, not establishing a hierarchy.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the tension between enforcing agency limits and respecting agency expertise can best be described as:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dismissive of the need for any judicial review of agency actions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Convinced that agency expertise should always prevail over statutory limits.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Recognizing it as an inherent feature of administrative law that courts must navigate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Highly critical of the Chevron deference framework.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Advocating that courts should never defer to agency interpretations.

explanations.correct: The author presents the tension matter-of-factly as something courts 'must navigate,' without taking a strong evaluative stance.
explanations.A: The passage describes how courts conduct review, suggesting the author accepts its necessity.
explanations.B: The passage indicates courts apply law strictly when statutes are clear, suggesting limits are important.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The author describes Chevron deference neutrally without criticism.
explanations.E: The passage describes deference as part of the established framework, not advocating against it.

questions.questionStem: The passage is organized primarily by:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Presenting conflicting theories about administrative law and defending one theory over the others.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Introducing a foundational principle, explaining how courts apply it, and describing the resulting tension with a competing principle.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Critiquing the doctrine of ultra vires and proposing a replacement framework.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tracing the historical development of administrative law from its origins to the present day.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Contrasting American administrative law with systems used in other countries.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces ultra vires, paragraph 2 explains judicial review procedures, and paragraph 3 describes the tension between enforcing agency limits and respecting expertise.
explanations.A: The passage presents the ultra vires doctrine and describes how it is applied, not defending it against competing theories.
explanations.C: The passage does not critique ultra vires or propose replacing it.
explanations.D: The passage describes the current framework but does not trace historical development.
explanations.E: The passage mentions Chevron deference (United States) but does not systematically compare other systems.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to 'Chevron deference' serves primarily to:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Illustrate a specific framework through which courts implement the principle of deference to agency expertise.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Argue that the doctrine of ultra vires should be abandoned.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Demonstrate that United States administrative law is superior to all other legal systems.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Criticize courts for deferring too much to agency interpretations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Show that agencies are the only arbiters of statutory meaning.

explanations.correct: The reference appears after the author discusses deference to agency expertise and serves as a named example of how this principle is operationalized in practice.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The passage describes ultra vires as a central principle and does not advocate its abandonment.
explanations.C: The passage does not compare different legal systems or claim superiority.
explanations.D: The reference is presented factually without critical commentary.
explanations.E: The passage indicates courts still assess whether interpretations are reasonable and based on statute.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following best describes how courts respond when they conclude an agency has exceeded its statutory authority?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They defer to the agency's interpretation as reasonable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They invalidate the agency action and order it to conform to the law.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They apply the doctrine of ultra vires without further review.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They defer to the agency's interpretation only if it is consistent with legislative history.

choices.label: E

explanations.correct: The passage states: 'If a court concludes that an agency exceeded its statutory authority, the court may invalidate the agency's action and order it to conform to the law.'
explanations.A: Deference applies when the court has not concluded the agency exceeded its authority.
explanations.C: Ultra vires is the principle used to identify the problem; the remedy is invalidation.
explanations.D: This describes a factor courts examine, not the remedy for exceeding authority.
explanations.E: Courts do not order legislatures to clarify statutes in the judicial system described.

passage:
Intellectual property law protects the rights of creators and inventors to control the use of their original works. Patent law, which is one branch of intellectual property protection, grants inventors exclusive rights to make, use, and sell their inventions for a limited period. This exclusivity provides inventors with economic incentives to develop and disclose new technologies. However, patent protection also creates a tension between the private interests of inventors and the public interest in accessing and building upon existing innovations.

A key limitation on patent rights is the doctrine of fair use, which permits others to use patented materials in certain contexts without obtaining permission from the patent holder. Fair use in patent law typically applies to research, education, and criticism. For example, a researcher may conduct experiments using a patented technology to understand how it works or to develop improvements, and this use would generally not constitute patent infringement. Similarly, educational institutions may use patented materials for teaching purposes within reasonable bounds. Courts have recognized that permitting such uses serves the broader public interest by advancing knowledge and fostering innovation.

However, determining the boundaries of fair use is frequently problematic. Patent holders argue that broad fair use exemptions undermine the economic incentives that patents are designed to provide, while fair use advocates contend that overly restrictive patent enforcement stifles follow-on innovation. Courts must therefore balance these competing interests when adjudicating disputes. Different jurisdictions have approached this balance differently, and the law continues to evolve as courts grapple with new factual scenarios involving patented technologies. What constitutes fair use in one context may not qualify as fair use in another, making predictability difficult for both patent holders and potential users.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patent law should eliminate fair use doctrine entirely in order to protect inventors' economic interests.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fair use doctrine permits unlimited copying of patented materials for any purpose.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patent protection provides incentives for innovation, but fair use doctrine creates tension between inventor rights and public access, and courts struggle to balance these competing interests.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Educational institutions have absolute right to use any patented materials for teaching purposes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patent law exists solely to advance the public interest in accessing technologies.

explanations.correct: The passage introduces patent protection and its purpose, explains fair use doctrine and its justification, and concludes by discussing the ongoing difficulty of balancing these competing interests.
explanations.A: The passage does not advocate eliminating fair use; it describes the balance courts must strike.
explanations.B: Fair use is described as limited to specific contexts (research, education, criticism), not unlimited.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The passage says educational use is permitted 'within reasonable bounds,' not absolutely.
explanations.E: Patent law is described as serving private inventor interests through exclusivity, not just public interest.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, fair use in patent law typically applies to:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Commercial manufacturing of patented products for profit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Research, education, and criticism.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any use that does not directly compete with the inventor's market.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Uses that generate revenue for the person conducting the activity.

choices.label: E
choices.text: All activities conducted by universities regardless of commercial nature.

explanations.correct: The passage explicitly states: 'Fair use in patent law typically applies to research, education, and criticism.'
explanations.A: Commercial manufacturing is associated with infringement, not fair use.
explanations.C: The passage does not describe fair use in terms of competitive impact.
explanations.D: Revenue generation is not mentioned as a criterion for fair use.
explanations.E: The passage indicates educational use is permitted 'within reasonable bounds,' implying limitations.

questions.questionStem: Based on the passage, it can be inferred that:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patent holders universally agree with fair use doctrine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Researchers conducting experiments with patented technology will sometimes infringe patents despite fair use protections.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fair use doctrine has eliminated the need for exclusive patent rights.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Courts have complete certainty about what uses qualify as fair use in all circumstances.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tension between patent rights and fair use cannot be resolved through judicial review.

explanations.correct: The passage notes that determining fair use boundaries is 'frequently problematic' and that 'what constitutes fair use in one context may not qualify as fair use in another'—suggesting borderline cases where infringement might occur.
explanations.A: The passage indicates patent holders argue that fair use exemptions undermine their interests.
explanations.C: Fair use is described as a limitation on patents, not as eliminating the need for them.
explanations.D: The passage states the law 'continues to evolve as courts grapple with new factual scenarios' and that predictability is difficult.
explanations.E: The passage indicates courts are actively adjudicating these disputes and balancing interests.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the balance between patent protection and fair use doctrine can best be described as:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wholly supportive of patent holders at the expense of fair use advocates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Completely opposed to any patent protection whatsoever.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Recognizing both interests as legitimate but acknowledging the difficulty courts face in balancing them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Convinced that fair use doctrine is always superior to patent rights.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Indifferent to whether patent or fair use interests are protected.

explanations.correct: The author presents both patent holders' and fair use advocates' concerns neutrally and acknowledges that courts 'must therefore balance these competing interests'—reflecting a measured view of both sides.
explanations.A: The author acknowledges fair use advocates' concerns about innovation stifling.
explanations.B: The author describes patent protection as providing important economic incentives.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The author states that patent holders argue fair use undermine incentives, suggesting legitimate concerns.
explanations.E: The author devotes most of the passage to exploring this balance, showing clear engagement.

questions.questionStem: The passage is organized primarily by:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Presenting evidence that patent law is more important than fair use doctrine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Introducing patent protection, explaining the fair use limitation, and then discussing challenges in balancing these principles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tracing the historical development of intellectual property law from ancient times to the present.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Comparing patent law in different countries and showing why one approach is superior.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Arguing that fair use doctrine should be eliminated in favor of absolute patent protection.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces patent protection and its purpose, paragraph 2 explains the fair use doctrine and its justification, and paragraph 3 discusses the challenge of balancing these interests.
explanations.A: The passage does not present evidence of relative importance; both are presented as legitimate.
explanations.C: The passage describes current law without historical development.
explanations.D: The passage mentions jurisdictional differences but does not systematically compare or evaluate systems.
explanations.E: The passage does not advocate for eliminating fair use doctrine.

questions.questionStem: The author's example of a researcher conducting experiments using a patented technology serves primarily to:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Demonstrate that researchers always violate patent law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Illustrate a context in which fair use doctrine permits use of patented materials without infringement.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Show that patent protection is unnecessary in research contexts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Argue that all research must be conducted by educational institutions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prove that fair use doctrine is always the most important consideration in patent disputes.

explanations.correct: The example appears immediately after fair use is introduced and serves to clarify what activities qualify as fair use, showing how the doctrine protects research activities.
explanations.A: The example indicates researchers do not infringe when using patented technology for research.
explanations.C: The example shows research is permitted to use patents, but does not address whether protection is necessary.
explanations.D: The example mentions a researcher but does not argue that all research must be institutional.
explanations.E: The example illustrates one application of fair use but not its universal supremacy.

questions.questionStem: The passage states that courts have recognized fair use doctrine serves the public interest by:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eliminating all patent protection for inventors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Permitting inventors to use any technology they wish without limitation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Advancing knowledge and fostering innovation through permitted uses of patented materials.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transferring all intellectual property rights to educational institutions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Preventing any commercial use of patented technologies.

explanations.correct: The passage states: 'Courts have recognized that permitting such uses serves the broader public interest by advancing knowledge and fostering innovation.'
explanations.A: Fair use is a limitation on patents, not elimination of them.
explanations.B: The passage describes limited fair use in specific contexts, not unlimited inventor use.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Transfer of rights to institutions is not mentioned in the passage.
explanations.E: Commercial use is not addressed; fair use involves research, education, and criticism.
